#3183. watchOS 27.3: Three new features coming soon to Apple Watch

watchOS 27.3 will launch to all users next month and introduce these three new Apple Watch features.

Siri AI keeps getting new features and also expanding to more languages. And in watchOS 27.3, the assistant will improve in both categories.

watchOS 27.3 upgrades Siri AI with new app actions across built-in apps like Calendar, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, and Weather. With these capabilities, Siri on your wrist can do more than ever.

There are also four new Siri AI languages supported in watchOS 27.3: Chinese (traditional), Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

For the latest Apple Watch models, watchOS 27.3 adds a new Audio Intelligence feature called Live Rewind. Per Apple’s website:

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

I’m curious to see how useful this proves in everyday life. When Apple demoed the feature in September, it showed Live Rewind being used at a restaurant when an Apple Watch user missed part of the server’s menu explanation. Asking the server to repeat what they said seems like an easier solution, but perhaps there are other occasions Live Rewind will come in handy.

It won’t be for everyone, but I’ve been testing watchOS 27.3’s new Siri Recap feature and really love it.

Siri Recap only works on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and it’s off by default. But if you have one of those models and enable the feature, Siri can create automatic logs of what’s happening in your day-to-day life.

Most of the time, you won’t need to reference any of the recaps and they’ll be automatically deleted after a week. But based on my experience with the feature, Siri Recap definitely comes in handy at times when trying to remember key details from conversations.

Which of watchOS 27.3’s new features are you most interested in? Let us know in the comments.

#3180. Apple offers a military discount, here’s how to get it

If you’re a member of the U.S. military, Apple offers an easy way to save 10% on eligible products and accessories. It’s available to current and veteran members of the U.S. military and their immediate family members living in the same household. While you’ll need to verify your eligibility to access the discount, the process is simple. There are also a few limitations you’ll want to know about before placing an order. Here’s everything you need to know.

A 10% discount is available to current and Veteran members of the US Military, National Guard and Reserve. Immediate family members who reside in the same household are also eligible.

Verification is handled through ID.me. Creating an ID.me account is free, and current military members can verify their service using their .mil email address. Veterans can enter details of their service information for ID.me to verify, or upload images of official documents (such as a DD-214) for ID.me to review and confirm their eligibility. Once you’re verified, your ID.me account can also be used to access military discounts from other retailers and services that support ID.me verification.

Once verified, you can start shopping by visiting Apple’s Store for Veterans and Military. The discount only applies to Apple products and accessories (including Beats) so third-party products aren’t eligible. Apple services, such as Apple Music and iCloud+, are also excluded. Orders can be shipped directly to you, or you can choose in-store pickup if the product is available at a nearby Apple Store.

This is probably the biggest catch. Apple specifically says ACMI isn’t available when shopping through the Veterans and Military Store. You can still earn 3% back in Daily Cash with Apple Card, but you lose the option to finance your purchase at 0% interest over several months. Apple Upgrade also isn’t available when purchasing through the military store.

The only way to get the military discount is to make your purchase through Apple’s website in a browser. The Apple Store app isn’t an option, which means you also can’t take advantage of Apple’s “Get Ready” feature to select your iPhone model, color, storage capacity, and carrier ahead of pre-orders opening. Instead, you’ll have to navigate Apple’s website on launch day, when demand is high and server traffic can make checkout more challenging. Whether the 10% savings is worth giving up the convenience of a potentially quicker checkout is ultimately up to you.

The military discount can’t be combined with carrier promotions or discounts on iPhone purchases. You can still trade in your existing iPhone through Apple and receive the applicable trade-in value, but you can’t take advantage of carrier-specific trade-in offers, like promotions that give you a larger credit when you trade in an eligible device and activate or upgrade a line.

These purchase limits reset on January 1 each year.

Apple’s military discount is a useful perk, especially if you’re buying a product at launch and want to save 10% right away. However, it’s worth comparing prices with other retailers before you buy, since sales and promotions can sometimes beat Apple’s discount. The military store also comes with a few limitations, so you’ll want to weigh the savings against the features and payment options you’re giving up. Even with those caveats, 10% off can make a real difference on an expensive Apple purchase.

#3179. Valens Semiconductor: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Valens is moving beyond premium chips into mainstream vehicles, cameras, and video gear, a shift that could widen its customer base over time.

On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 11, 2026, Valens Semiconductor (VLN -11.73%) announced quarterly revenue of $21.9 million, topping management's outlook. The chipmaker is shifting its core business strategy from selling high-end specialized silicon toward capturing higher-volume mainstream markets. Three takeaways from the call highlight how this strategic pivot alters the company's long-term thesis.

The company historically targeted niche, high-performance audio-video installations with premium connectivity chips. To accelerate growth, management launched the VS6310 semiconductor chip designed for lower power consumption, allowing direct integration into standard video conferencing equipment.

In automotive connectivity, high costs limited adoption of the company's MIPI A-PHY standard, an industry specification for vehicle sensor data, to luxury vehicles. A collaboration with onsemi, a semiconductor manufacturing partner, integrates connectivity directly into 3-megapixel image sensors, removing stand-alone serializer chips to reduce overall component costs for mass-market vehicles.

Valens previously captured revenue solely from selling individual silicon chips to device manufacturers. By leveraging Acroname, its hardware engineering subsidiary acquired in 2024, the business is assembling complete active cables and extension boxes to capture higher sales value across the supply chain.

Automotive shipments to Mercedes-Benz are expanding, and the company is tracking toward the upper boundary of its annual sales target. Integrating semiconductor designs directly with key manufacturing partners reinforces structural switching costs across broader volume markets.

Expanding into mainstream categories broadens market scale while custom software layers increase customer retention. Scaling system-level products secures long-term growth across both core segments.

#3175. 5 Ways to Spend Less on Healthcare in Retirement

With the right strategy, you can keep your costs down.

Retirement is supposed to be a time to enjoy the money you've spent decades saving. But there's one expense that can make that difficult -- healthcare.

As a retiree, you'll have to budget for doctor visits, prescriptions, medical procedures, and insurance premiums. And while Medicare provides important coverage for Americans ages 65 and older, it doesn't mean healthcare becomes free.

In fact, healthcare could become your biggest senior expense, especially if you have chronic medical problems you're managing. The good news, though, is that the right strategies could help you keep your healthcare spending down. Here are five ways to ease that burden and preserve your retirement savings.

One of the most expensive mistakes retirees can make is missing their initial Medicare enrollment window. Most Americans become eligible for Medicare at age 65, but your initial enrollment period spans seven months. It begins three months before the month you turn 65 and ends three months after that month.

If you don't enroll on time, you could face a lifelong 10% surcharge on your Medicare Part B premiums for each 12-month period you could've had coverage but failed to sign up. Over the course of a long retirement, those surcharges could amount to a lot of wasted money.

Now, there are exceptions for people who continue working and have qualifying employer-sponsored health insurance. But before you delay your Medicare enrollment, check with your HR department if you're still working, or with your health plan administrator, to make sure you truly have creditable coverage that makes waiting safe.

The Medicare plan you start out with isn't guaranteed to be the most cost-effective one for life. Medicare Advantage and Part D drug plans can change their premiums, deductibles, and covered medications and benefits from one year to the next. So it's important to review your choices annually during open enrollment.

Medicare's annual open enrollment period runs from Oct. 15 through Dec. 7 each year. During this window, beneficiaries can switch Medicare Advantage or Part D plans.

When assessing your choices, don't just look at premiums. A plan with a lower monthly premium isn't automatically cheaper.

Another way to avoid unnecessary healthcare expenses is by understanding exactly what your Medicare plan covers. This is particularly important if you're enrolled in Medicare Advantage, since these plans often have specific requirements that can impact your costs.

Medicare Advantage plans require members to use doctors within a designated provider network. Visiting an out-of-network provider could result in higher costs or no coverage at all, depending on the plan.

Prior authorization is another important consideration. Certain procedures may require approval before treatment. If you don't get that approval, you could face coverage denials or unexpected bills.

Before scheduling an appointment, undergoing a procedure, or filling a prescription, verify your coverage and know what steps you need to take. Understanding your plan's rules could prevent unpleasant financial surprises.

The nice thing about original Medicare is that you can see any provider in the country who takes Medicare as insurance. But if you'll be skipping Medicare Advantage and sticking with original Medicare, it pays to buy supplemental insurance, or Medigap, early on.

Medicare enrollees can face high deductibles, coinsurance, and other out-of-pocket costs. Medigap could help cover these expenses, helping you avoid financial strain. And while Medigap plans do require an additional monthly premium, they can provide greater predictability when budgeting for healthcare.

The best time to purchase Medigap coverage is generally during the six-month window that begins when you're 65 or older and are enrolled in Medicare Part B. During this period, insurers generally cannot deny coverage or charge more because of preexisting conditions.

When it comes to paying for healthcare, don't assume that the first price you're quoted is the lowest available. Prescription drug costs are a particularly important place to look for savings.

If you're facing hefty copays, ask your doctors and pharmacists whether a lower-cost generic medication is available. It also pays to compare prescription prices at different pharmacies, review your plan's preferred pharmacy network, and ask whether mail-order options offer savings.

Healthcare expenses may be unavoidable in retirement, but that doesn't mean you have to strain your budget to afford them. A little research, careful Medicare planning, and a willingness to ask questions could help you keep more of your savings without skimping on care.

#3172. Alcon Inc. (ALC) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Alcon narrows 2026 guidance as its Neurotech retina deal closes.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Alcon Inc. (ALC -2.16%) reported third-quarter net sales of $2.7 billion, representing 5% growth year over year. Management narrowed its full-year 2026 guidance, forecasting approximately 6% sales growth and 12% to 14% core diluted EPS growth. While the Surgical segment benefited from 11% growth in equipment revenue, the Implantables sub-segment faced a 2% decline due to competitive activity in the U.S. premium intraocular lens market. The company acquired Neurotech Pharmaceuticals for $550 million to expand its retina portfolio, targeting peak sales between $250 million and $400 million for the newly acquired treatment for Macular Telangiectasia Type 2. Core operating margin expanded 150 basis points to 21.8%, aided by $60 million in nonrecurring tariff refunds and ongoing manufacturing efficiencies.

Before we begin, please note that our press release, presentation and remarks today will include forward-looking statements, including statements regarding our future outlook. They should be considered in addition to and not as a substitute for IFRS prescribed performance measures. Reconciliation between our non-IFRS measures and the most directly comparable IFRS measures can be found in our earnings press release. For discussion purposes, our comments on growth, growth rates are expressed in constant currency.

In a moment, David will begin with highlights from the third quarter. After his remarks, Tim will walk through our financial performance in the quarter and outlook for the remainder of the year. David will then return with closing comments before we open the line for Q&A. With that, I'll turn the call over to our CEO, David Endicott.

As I reflect on the quarter, we saw good momentum across several parts of the portfolio. In Surgical, equipment and consumables remain strong, particularly in the U.S., where demand for UNITY and Valeda continue to be robust, while Implantables continued to grow in our international markets, but that growth was offset by competitive pressures in the U.S.

And in Vision Care, contact lenses and ocular health, both delivered solid growth, driven by share gains in contact lenses, Tryptyr and Systane. Now Tim will take you through the detailed financials. So let me focus on what's driving the business and why we remain confident about the opportunities ahead. Underpinning our conviction that we can continue to grow faster than the market is a steady cadence of innovation, supported by clinical evidence that differentiates our products. At this fall's major congresses, we shared new data demonstrating the benefits of our latest technologies for surgeons, eye care professionals and patients.

At ESCRS, we presented new data reinforcing the unsurpassed near vision performance of PanOptix Pro and the surgical efficiency of UNITY VCS. And at the optometry and ophthalmology annual meetings in the U.S., we shared new data showing Systane Pro delivered symptom relief clinically comparable to the prescription product MIEBO, with the accessibility and convenience of an over-the-counter option. In addition, new research on Tryptyr and dry eye showed clinically meaningful improvements in patients' ability to work and perform daily activities with more than 70% reporting satisfaction with digital device use and end-of-day comfort. We also highlighted Valeda, the first and only FDA-approved treatment for early and intermediate dry AMD.

We continue to build awareness among ophthalmologists and engage the broader eye care community to identify appropriate patients and broaden access to this important new treatment. Together, these data reinforce the differentiation of our newest products and support our efforts to translate that innovation into sustainable revenue growth. We're seeing that innovation translate into commercial momentum in equipment where UNITY VCS and CS, along with the Valeda drove double-digit growth. In the U.S., UNITY continues to gain significant traction at some of the nation's most prominent academic medical centers with placements secured in 40% of U.S. teaching hospitals in the past year alone.

Importantly, when combined with our legacy platform, our equipment is now available in 98% of ophthalmology teaching programs, providing broad exposure to the next generation of surgeons. Turning to Implantables. Sales were down 2% and with IOLs down 1%, driven primarily by competitive launches in the U.S. premium IOL category and continued reimbursement challenges for dual procedures in glaucoma implants. In the U.S., competitive trialing and sampling of IOLs remain significant, and we expect that activity to continue through the early part of next year. At the same time, we are strengthening our competitive position with the next wave of innovation in our IOL portfolio Vivity Pro.

Vivity Pro received FDA approval in the U.S. in early November with CE Mark expected soon. This lens was uniquely designed to improve near and intermediate vision without sacrificing distance or contrast. Our clinical data package at launch will include direct comparisons to competitive lenses. And we began the U.S. KOL release last week and look forward to the full launch in January with expansion into select European markets to follow during the first quarter. Additionally, TruPlus, our first entrant in the Monofocal Plus segment is now broadly available in the U.S. and rolling out across Europe. Looking forward, our experience in Europe gives us confidence in how these competitive dynamics can evolve.

Competitive launches there have now been in the market for some time and with PanOptix Pro as our response, we returned to growth and are regaining PC-IOL share. That provides an encouraging reference point as we prepare for the full U.S. and European launches of Vivity Pro in January. More broadly, we believe this next wave of innovation can strengthen our performance well beyond the near term. PanOptix Pro, Vivity Pro and TruPlus are the beginning of a steady cadence of new IOL technologies that we believe will position us to drive sustainable above-market growth. Turning to contact lenses.

We continue to gain share in the U.S. across both DAILIES and reusable supported by the breadth of our water innovations portfolio. That performance is an important example of our ability to win through differentiated innovation and commercial execution. The underlying market continues to benefit from premiumization as consumers move towards daily disposables and specialty lenses. The TOTAL and PRECISION families give us premium and high-performance platforms while innovations such as TOTAL30 Multifocal for astigmatism expand our reach into higher-value specialty segments. We remain well positioned to drive continued share and value growth. Finally, in ocular health, execution remains strong across both our prescription and consumer dry eye franchises.

Tryptyr continues to build momentum, reaching approximately 6% market share as of October. We've also recently initiated direct-to-consumer promotion to increase patient awareness and drive demand. We're making solid progress against our reimbursement objectives with now more than 2/3 of commercial lives covered. On the consumer side, Systane delivered another quarter of double-digit growth led by our multi-dose preservative-free formulations including Systane Pro as we continue to gain share in a fast-growing market. We're also continuing to broaden our consumer eye care portfolio. Just a few weeks ago, the FDA approved BRYTLY, our new redness reliever eye drop. BRYTLY works in just 1 minute and provides up to 12 hours of redness reduction, lasting up to 50% longer than Lumify.

We expect BRYTLY to be available at major retailers and online in the first quarter. Before turning to the market environment, let me highlight an important addition to our retina portfolio. We recently acquired Neurotech Pharmaceuticals, adding ENCELTO, the first and only FDA-approved treatment for Macular Telangiectasia Type 2 or MacTel. This is a rare and progressive retinal disease that can cause irreversible central vision loss. ENCELTO is an encapsulated cell therapy that is intended for surgical intravitreal implantation. Neurotech is strategically compelling because it sits at the intersection of cell therapy, pharmaceuticals and surgery, and it plays directly to Alcon's leadership in surgical retina.

There are approximately 25,000 diagnosed MacTel patients in the U.S. today with an additional 2,000 to 3,000 newly diagnosed each year, and coverage is largely established. By combining Neurotech's differentiated technology and cell therapy capabilities with Alcon's commercial reach and retina relationships, we believe we can broaden access and build an important new long-term growth platform. We expect peak sales between $250 million to $400 million with the ultimate trajectory largely dependent on how quickly patients are identified and brought into treatment. We're excited to welcome the Neurotech team and believe the acquisition strengthens both our retina franchise and the diversification of Alcon's future growth. Turning briefly to our efforts with Aurion.

We're pleased to report enrollment is complete in our pivotal Phase III program, and we remain on track for a 2027 FDA submission and a 2028 FDA approval decision. Before I close, let me share a few observations about the market environment. Let me start with contact lenses. Globally, the market remains healthy, growing in line with our assumptions at approximately 4% to 5% with roughly 3 points coming from price and 2 points from mix. The U.S. remains the strongest market growing approximately 5% to 6%. Growth outside the U.S. is more modest, particularly in Europe, where online channels and private label brands continue to put pressure on pricing, although mix remains positive.

Across markets, the important trend is continued premiumization as consumers move toward daily disposables and specialty lenses. That shift supports positive mix and plays directly to the strength of our portfolio in these higher-value categories. In cataract, procedure growth remains in line with our assumptions and below historical levels, reflecting capacity constraints in the U.S. and reimbursement and hospital economics internationally. At the same time, premiumization remains a meaningful source of value growth, and we believe the strength and breadth of our premium IOL portfolio positions us well to capitalize on this trend. U.S. advanced technology IOL penetration reached 21.9%, up 160 basis points year-over-year, while international penetration increased 60 basis points to approximately 16%.

And across our other eye care markets, underlying trends remain healthy and in line with our expectations. So when we put all that together, we estimate that our aggregate markets grew approximately 3% in the third quarter at the low end of our assumptions underlying our guidance. Looking ahead, our base case assumes these trends broadly continue into next year, and our focus remains on execution, innovation and premiumization across the business. The breadth of our portfolio and the impact of our innovation continue to differentiate us, enabling us to grow faster than the market. So in closing, we remain on track to deliver on our full year guidance.

While our underlying markets are at the low end of our original guidance assumptions, it's our responsibility to deliver through that environment. And we're doing that by executing our launches, translating innovation into broader adoption and driving premiumization and entering attractive new white spaces. We have a diversified portfolio that continues to get stronger, including the addition of Neurotech in retinal disease. This gives us multiple avenues to outgrow our markets and drive durable earnings growth and long-term shareholder value. With that, I'll turn it over to Tim, who will walk you through the financial details of the quarter.

Timothy Stonesifer: Thanks, David. Beginning with the top line, our third quarter sales were $2.7 billion, up 5% versus prior year and up 6% on a year-to-date basis. While the cadence of growth was slightly different than we anticipated due to specific areas of competitive pressure, we remain on track with the midpoint of the original guidance provided in February and expect to grow approximately 6% for the year. In our surgical franchise, sales were up 4% year-over-year to $1.5 billion. Implantable sales were $422 million in the quarter, down 2% versus the prior year. Within this, IOLs were down 1% due primarily to competitive launches, particularly in the U.S.

As David mentioned, PanOptix continued to perform well and the family was up 9% year-over-year, growing nicely in all regions. This growth was driven by strong customer demand and continued commercial execution. In consumables, third quarter sales of $789 million were up 6%. This growth was driven by procedural volumes, price increases and Valeda. In equipment, sales were $269 million in the quarter and up 11%. This growth was driven by continued momentum from our UNITY platform and the strength of our Valeda launch despite now lapping the UNITY VCS launch in the prior year. Turning to Vision Care. Third quarter sales were $1.2 billion and up 6%. Contact lens sales increased 5% to $737 million.

This performance reflects continued premium trade-up, share gains and price increases, partially offset by declines in legacy products. In Ocular Health, third quarter sales were $500 million, up 8% versus prior year. Systane grew double digits, supported by share gains and strength across our preservative-free portfolio with Systane Pro revenue doubling year-over-year. This growth was partially offset by continued softness in contact lens care. Moving down the income statement. Third quarter core gross margin was 65.7%, up 280 basis points year-over-year. As we communicated last quarter, the increase was expected and largely driven by tariff refunds along with continued manufacturing efficiencies. Core operating income was $591 million and 21.8% of sales, up 150 basis points versus the prior year.

This improvement was largely driven by the tariff refunds I just mentioned and was partially offset by higher sales and marketing spend. Below the operating line, interest expense was $52 million during the quarter, broadly in line with the prior year. Turning to taxes. Our core effective tax rate was 17.8% in the third quarter, up from 16.9% in the prior year. Our year-to-date core effective tax rate was 19.4%, which is broadly in line with our guidance. Finally, core diluted earnings per share were $0.91 in the quarter, up 15% versus prior year. Turning to cash.

We generated more than $1.3 billion of free cash flow in the first 9 months, which enabled a return of $748 million to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases over the same period. Within the quarter, we returned $210 million to shareholders through our share repurchase program and have now completed more than 1/3 of our $1.5 billion repurchase authorization. Moving to our outlook for 2026. Based on recent market trends, we now assume that aggregate eye care markets grew 3% for the year and exchange rates as of the end of October hold through year-end.

We also assume the tariffs currently applicable to Alcon's business remain in effect through year-end, including U.S. import tariff rates of approximately 10% to 12.5%. Based on these assumptions and our performance through the first 9 months, our guidance for 2026 is as follows: we expect sales growth of approximately 6%, consistent with the midpoint of our original guidance issued in February. On profitability, we are narrowing our expected core operating margin expansion to a range of 100 to 150 basis points, while also narrowing our range on core diluted EPS growth to 12% to 14%. Moving to 2027.

We will be issuing formal guidance in February, but I wanted to provide some color on the headwinds and tailwinds we see heading into next year. Starting with the underlying market, our base case assumption is that the current market trends that David referenced persist through next year. On the top line, starting with Surgical, although we expect equipment to grow next year, it will be the primary headwind as we lap the 2026 UNITY rollout. However, the launches of UNITY M and UNITY DX, along with continued expansion of our Valeda installed base, will help alleviate some of the pressure.

In implantables, we expect to return to growth given the launches of Vivity Pro and TruPlus as well as the continued momentum from PanOptix Pro. And in Vision Care, our recent and upcoming launches, including Tryptyr and BRYTLY, will continue to contribute to growth, while the addition of Neurotech is expected to add approximately 75 to 100 basis points to the top line. Overall, we expect another year of above-market sales growth in 2027. Moving down the income statement. Historically, we've been able to get approximately 100 to 150 basis points of operating leverage by growing revenue faster than our cost base.

Next year, we'd expect to drive roughly 150 to 200 basis points of leverage given the additional efficiency measures we implemented in 2026. However, we will face some headwinds in 2027. First, our 2026 results included $60 million in tariff refunds and a $15 million milestone payment, both of which are nonrecurring. In addition, we expect pressure from incremental inflation related to memory and resins as well as some near-term pressure from the Neurotech acquisition. Despite these headwinds, we continue to expect margin improvement in 2027 and we'll give you more color in February when we finalize our budget. Before we wrap up, I want to highlight an upcoming new accounting standard.

IFRS 18 becomes effective in January and will introduce changes to the presentation and classification of certain items in our financial statements, including some of our key metrics. We'll provide more information on the impact of the new standard when we report it in February, including select historical financial information, reflecting the new presentation to support comparability and modeling. In conclusion, we are performing in line with the expectations we set at the beginning of the year. Our year-to-date sales are up 6%, core diluted EPS is up double digits, and we again demonstrated the free cash flow potential of this business while executing on our commitment to meaningful capital returns.

These results reflect the durability of our business, our clear market leadership, and the efforts of our associates around the world. With that, I'll turn it back to David.

David Endicott: Thanks, Tim. As we approach the end of the year, I remain confident about the trajectory of the business. Our innovation pipeline continues to strengthen. We're executing with discipline, and we're continuing to modernize our go-to-market approach. We're on track to complete a restructuring to improve operational efficiency. We strengthened our portfolio with the addition of Neurotech and we have already returned approximately $750 million to shareholders. And none of this would be possible without the hard work of our more than 25,000 associates around the world who help people see brilliantly every day. With that, operator, please open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question is from Anthony Petrone with Mizuho.

Anthony Petrone: Maybe, David, one on equipment and -- and then just on BRYTLY. When we think about the rate of UNITY VCS installs, it looks like it's tracking on schedule, roughly 3,000 units a year. But I think when you initially put that trajectory out, there was a little bit of a step-up in 2027 for installs. So should we be thinking that there's another bolus that can come in '27 versus 2026 and just in terms of the number of installations? And then just on BRYTLY, I know the launch is 1Q, but should we be expecting any kind of big stocking orders in 4Q ahead of that large retail launch in 1Q?

David Endicott: Thanks, Anthony. On the equipment piece, I think you should think about it as relatively similar to this year in terms of unit placements. I think maybe this year was a big year for VCS and CS got out the gate. I think probably full speed maybe second quarter. So I think we've got a little bit more step-up in CS as opposed to VCS. So remember that the CS market is much bigger. So again, I think there'll be a bit of a mix shift to CS next year as we sell probably a good bit more of that versus VCS. But largely, I would say the units are similar, I would say.

I think the -- on the BRYTLY launch, we have got retail orders. I don't think we're going to ship that until next year. And so I would not count on anything in the fourth quarter, but we are excited about that product. It is kind of a new market area for us, and we've been looking for white spaces like this. So again, this product lasts longer than the market leader, and we're excited about the potential of that with the consumer.

Operator: Our next question is from Brett Fishbin with KeyBanc Capital Markets Inc.

Brett Fishbin: I just wanted to ask one first on -- just to clarify some of the margin commentary for 2027. I think you mentioned potentially driving 150 to 200 basis points of leverage and then walk through a couple of considerations. I wanted to just understand if the 150 to 200 basis points is net of some of those expected headwinds or if you're talking about like 150 to 200 basis points of underlying improvement before some of those headwinds?

Timothy Stonesifer: Yes. I think about that as more of a gross number before the adjustment. So if you think -- if you look at historically, we've always said 100 to 150 basis points of improvement. We think it will be higher next year given the efficiency program that we implemented. So if you start with 150 to 200 basis points, I then start subtracting the pressures that we're going to see from the one-offs that we saw in 2026 that don't recur. We do anticipate seeing a little bit more inflationary pressure and then a little bit of pressure -- near-term pressure for the Neurotech acquisition.

Brett Fishbin: All right. Super helpful. And then just on Implantables, it seemed like growth took a little bit of a step back this quarter. It sounded like it was more specific to the U.S. I was hoping you could just expand maybe on what you saw incremental from 1H levels that caused a little bit of further erosion? And then just level of confidence in your remarks, do you expect a return to growth next year with some of the new product launches?

David Endicott: Yes, I think you're right. I mean, actually, the step forward was international. So Europe, I think, gained share in the quarter. But there was an extraordinary amount of activity -- competitive activity in the third quarter, and there'll be more in the fourth quarter, I think. So we're going to see some continued competitive activity that surgeons want to try new products and good companies bring products out. They're going to try them. And so I think we felt like that was certainly part of the challenge. But it wasn't way off of where we've been. It was a little bit off of where we've been in the prior quarters.

So I think we're just kind of working our way through to the next launches. And I think as I said in my remarks, Vivity Pro is a really exciting product for us. I think what we've -- and we've got it approved now. So I think we've got it in the hands of a number of KOLs right now. We'll get -- and we've got very good data comparing it to the competitor who is most active right now. So I think we feel like we're in a good place with better near vision, better intermediate than the competition and with very similar contrast and distance.

So that data, I think, makes us confident that when we get it out full speed next year, we'll see this thing continue. I would also point out that TruPlus is just kind of getting its feet around the world, and that's our new entry into the Monofocal Plus space. And PanOptix Pro is still getting going internationally. So I think if you look around the world at where our portfolio is, and frankly, we've got a number of products after that which are on their way. We feel very confident over the next several years that we're going to be in a solid position for Implantables.

Operator: Our next question is from Julien Ouaddour with Bank of America.

Julien Ouaddour: I have one question and one was keeping a follow-up. So the question I just want to clarify your comment about UNITY, where you expect the same volume next year, but the shift to CS, which I believe the ASP is lower. I just want to make sure that you expect the revenue in absolute terms in equipment to grow next year given the mix shift? And the follow-up, maybe I can ask it right now. Could you just help us to disaggregate the growth contribution from Valeda in the quarter? I mean how much did Valeda contribute to the 11% growth in equipment and the 6% growth in consumables?

David Endicott: Yes, Julien, we don't break up the individual products in the categories, but I would just say that the category growth in equipment we were pleased with. I may -- you may have misheard me or I may have mis-said it. I think the way to think about UNITY is that the mix will shift to CS in aggregate. The value growth will be greater than it was in the prior year, principally because the CS market is much bigger than the retina market. So the retina market, I don't know, is maybe 1.5 million procedures, 2 million procedures, the cataract market is 5 million or 6 million in the U.S. and around the world, it's much bigger.

So I think we have a much bigger market to address with CS, and I suspect we'll do quite well with CS.

Operator: Our next question is from Larry Biegelsen with Wells Fargo.

Larry Biegelsen: I had one on '27 and one on Neurotech. So Tim, maybe if we could -- what's the net impact of what you said on revenue? How will growth in '27 compared to '26? Are you pointing to basically, you call it 5% organic growth, plus 75 to 100 basis points for Neurotech? And margins, you talked about a lot of headwinds. So should we be thinking about -- but you also said some margin improvement. So should we be thinking about 50 basis points of improvement? And I have one follow-up.

Timothy Stonesifer: Yes. I'm not going to give guidance here today, Larry. But you're thinking about it correctly. Listen, we think the markets are going to hang in there at about 3%, as David said in the prepared remarks. We don't anticipate -- we're not expecting any uplift from that. As we've always said, we think we can grow faster than the market. We feel very good about the innovation pipeline and the launches that we have coming up and that are in place now. So we'd expect to grow faster than that market. And then to your point, I would add 75 to 100 basis points on that for Neurotech. As far as the margin expansion, those are the pressure points.

I think we hit those. We do expect margin expansion next year and we'll give you more color on that. We're going to continue to get some margin expansion out of our marketing and sales area as we've done historically. But you're not going to see a net number of 100 to 150 basis points that we've talked about before. And we'll give you more color in February.

Larry Biegelsen: Very helpful. On Neurotech, I mean, ENCELTO, it seems like a sleeper based on our checks. So what our 2026 sales and the 75 to 100 basis points for '27, it sounds like -- it wasn't clear if that was Vision Care or total Alcon? But even if it's total Alcon, I think if I'm doing the math right, it's $50 million, which seems small. And just lastly, how are you thinking about the ramp to those peak sales of $275 million to $400 million? I mean, even the midpoint there implies only about 750 patients or 1,500 eyes per year?

David Endicott: Yes, Larry, you're doing the math the same way we are. Let me just tell you the dynamic we're trying to manage. What we're trying to manage is this is a new -- we've been involved in this for now a few months and trying to understand exactly the pace at which patients can be found and brought into treatment is really the kind of key variable here. And until we get a really clean view of what that looks like, we feel comfortable with the 250 to 400 range. I do -- I understand the math you're doing, and I do understand that, that could be the case.

I think what we're going to find is that these patients -- there's a certain number of centers that are prepared to do this surgery. These are infrequently found patients and the pace at which we find them get them to treatment, get them through the reimbursement system will be the defining factor. Now you could be right and we could be wrong on this one, but I think we're going to be careful around this as we go forward.

Timothy Stonesifer: I would just say, Larry, on 2027, that I would apply that 75 to 100 basis points on the total Alcon revenue.

Operator: Our next question is from Veronika Dubajova with Citi.

Veronika Dubajova: I have two, please. The first was -- I just want to come back on the moving pieces for margin, Tim. And I guess this year, you stepped up DTC by about $40 million sort of spending some of the proceeds from the tariff refunds. Just curious if this is something you intend to continue into next year? Or should we put that into the tailwind column as we think about the margin piece for on 2027? And then my second question is on contact lenses. And David, your thoughts on kind of the health of the market and your ability to outgrow it. Obviously, the gap between you and the market has narrowed pretty substantially this year.

I know you've had some headwinds in terms of discontinuation of some older product lines. But it'd be good to understand sort of, one, how you're thinking about market growth contact lenses for next year; and two, your ability to outperform that from a share gain perspective?

Timothy Stonesifer: Veronika, thanks for the question. Listen, it's really hard to say if the $40 million of additional spend is recurring, given that our total SG&A base is $3.5 billion. So I think -- but I get your point, I think the way to think about it is take the 150 to 200 basis points that we talked about back out the pressures that I just mentioned. Most of that is going to be in the gross margin line. If you think about the refunds and the milestone payments and the inflation. However, we're still expecting to get margin expansion next year, and most of that will come from, as I said, M&S and a little bit from G&A.

So we will continue to expect to get leverage out of the M&S line.

David Endicott: Veronika, the global contact lens market was probably 4% to 5%. It was healthy in the U.S., probably 5% to 6% with maybe 3% price and 2% mix. But international contact market was softer as a function of online channels and the private label business. It was probably in that kind of 1% to 2% range. So we grew a share point on the quarter or roughly a share point. We continue to outperform the market in that space. And I think we're feeling pretty good about it right now, principally because we kind of rotated back towards DAILIES and specialty lenses, and the reason for that, obviously, is those are the fastest-growing segments of the market.

We had a good run in a reusable market. We took some share back there. Those are very profitable businesses for us. And now I think we see the market as growing principally in this premiumization process of moving people up. That's been the case for a while, but it continues on very successfully, I think, in the U.S. And again, the international business was grown principally by mix. So you get less price there, but more mix, and we're trying to play that particular trend right now.

Operator: Our next question is from Ryan Zimmerman with U.S. Bancorp. BTIG.

Ryan Zimmerman: Tim, if we look at '27, I appreciate all the color, but as I think about kind of the continued double-digit core EPS growth, I'm just curious what's coming from, say, operating leverage versus revenue growth versus share count reduction? And again, knowing that you didn't give double-digit core EPS growth as a guide, but assuming that, that's the case.

Timothy Stonesifer: Yes. Again, as you know, the revenue growth really drives the operating leverage. So assuming that we can grow faster than the market, we would expect to get the margin expansion that I talked to a little bit earlier and that will drop down to EPS growth. I wouldn't -- from a year-over-year basis from a share count and buyback, I wouldn't expect anything significantly different than what we did this year. But again, we'll evaluate that as we do when we look at our capital allocation strategy. And it just really depends on what M&A is out there, how much cash we have, but we will put the cash to work.

Ryan Zimmerman: Okay. And then on Implantables, down 2% this quarter flat year-to-date on a constant currency basis. David, can you help us maybe size the market share loss in your view? And is it concentrated in a specific product area, whether that's EDOF or monofocal versus maybe what's happening in the market?

David Endicott: Yes, sure, sure. I mean look, the total foldables for us globally was actually flat in volume. It was AT-IOLs, and it was really U.S. So if you look at the international markets, we gained share in Europe. U.S., we lost some share in the PC-IOL market. And the monofocal business, again, we actually gained a small amount. So our general view is volumes are pretty healthy still because we basically were flat this quarter on volume. But you can't give up the AT-IOL share because it's obviously more valuable. So this premiumization play that I think exists in that market, we need to get on the front foot with.

So again, I feel very good about what's going on in Europe with PanOptix Pro and what's moving around the world with Pro. We're going to -- we're hoping to see that very same thing happen with Vivity Pro as we come back in on top of these competitive launches.

Operator: Our next question is from Jeff Johnson with Baird.

Jeffrey Johnson: So Tim, I guess one clarifying question, a lot of focus on 2027 for all the right reasons. But the approximate 6% for this year in the updated guidance, that approximate could be doing a decent amount of heavy lifting, I guess, trying to back into what you expect for 4Q. If I go right to 6%, I'd be kind of pushing about 100 basis points improvement versus 3Q. Are you implying in the updated guidance a little bit of improvement in growth versus 3Q? Or should we be thinking 3Q is kind of the run rate at least for now? And then one follow-up.

Timothy Stonesifer: Yes. Listen, the reason we went with approximate is because we don't see 5% in play and we don't see 7% in play. So we thought approximately 6% was kind of how we're looking at it right now. As far as -- again, I'm not going to guide Q4 revenue, but your thinking is the right thinking. And just keep in mind, there will be some Neurotech in there. So that's why you might see a little bit more of a jump up, but we would expect to see some improvement in Q4.

Jeffrey Johnson: All right. Fair enough. And then, David, you talked -- you've said a couple of different things on VCS, CS. I just want to clarify what you've said. I know you don't guide product line. But again, I guess the question is you do expect it sounds like VCS, CS combined unit growth next year, offset by negative mix, but then I think you used the word value. I just want to make sure you are expecting VCS, CS combined UNITY platform revenue growth next year and then on top of that, a little bit of M&DX and Valeda contribution so that equipment growth does have a positive sign on it next year.

David Endicott: Yes, it does in both. So growth in total units will be higher than it was this year because the CS mix will help it, growth in total dollars will be up next year, but it will be a little bit less than the unit growth because obviously, we're getting a lower ASP on average if you mix to CS versus VCS. Hopefully, that helps.

Operator: Our next question is from Chris Pasquale with Barclays.

Christopher Pasquale: One on Neurotech, just how soon after diagnosis do patients need to start therapy in order to see a benefit? I'm just wondering how much penetration into that prevalence pool, the peak sales estimate assumes versus just achieving some broad use in the annual incidence rate.

David Endicott: This is a very slow moving disorder, and it takes years to lose as much central vision as you ultimately will. However, as soon as you're diagnosed, historically, there hasn't been a therapy to treat this. And so I'm not sure I know the answer precisely to your question other than I think we have a pool of patients who have been diagnosed. We kind of know who they are. We need to get them to a surgeon who is willing to do this and then have them through the system work through the reimbursement part of this thing and then also get them to a center that will do the surgery.

So more -- the logistics of this, I think, are the piece that we're still working our way through I think we have a sense that there are plenty of patients and patients that we can find. I think it is a matter of then how do we get them to the right surgeon who knows how to do this, is trained to do it in a center that will do it and again, this isn't like cataract surgery, where they're doing 1,000 a year. This is 1 or 2 or 3. And so it's a novel procedure to many surgical centers.

Christopher Pasquale: That's helpful. And then you talked about premiumization in both contacts and IOLs. In some other corners in med tech, we've heard some rumblings recently about increased economic sensitivity due to cost of living pressures. It certainly doesn't sound like you're seeing that yet. But as you think about '27, how confident are you that price and mix can continue to be such significant contributors to your market growth?

David Endicott: Well, when I think about -- I don't know that price is going to be a big piece of it. I do think mix will be. And I think we would look at that and we'd say we've run sensitivities and tried to correlate consumer confidence with revenue growth in both contact lenses and AT-IOLs, for example, or even OTC products. You just don't see that big of a correlation. Over long periods of time, there's almost none in short windows, there may be a little bit, but I think there's principally something to ignore there on the consumer side.

I think you can see that even in the first -- in this current quarter where we had very significant AT-IOL growth in penetration, up almost 2 points in the Americas, up 0.5 point, 50 basis points in international. So globally, very significant penetration. The same thing with kind of contact lenses. You saw continued movement of the highest value lenses. The DAILIES, I think we're growing high single digits as opposed to the rest of the market, which was growing roughly in the 5% range. So I think that is -- we're pretty comfortable with the premiumization. I'd be a little more cautious on price and how that plays out.

Operator: Our next question is from Graham Doyle with UBS.

Graham Doyle: Just one quick clarification and then one on the midterm guide. Sorry, I know it's come up a few times, but just to double check because we've had some incoming from investors here. David, your comments on UNITY, you expect using VCS and CS to sell more volume next year than this year? Just to clarify that. And then a question on the midterm guide. So on the 6% to 8% constant currency, you obviously weren't in the range last year, you'll be at the bottom end of this year. How do we think about the relevance of this guide going forward into next year, given where market growth is?

It just be useful to know that so when we kind of go back to our models. So how we think about that.

David Endicott: Yes. I obviously wasn't particularly clear on this VCS, CS thing. We are going to grow in total units, and we are going to grow in total dollars. But the mix will be more to the CS side. Is that relatively clear?

David Endicott: Okay. Great. And then look, on the long-term guide, obviously, we -- during this stretch, market growth has been more modest. And given last year's performance and where we are this year, and where we think going forward, we still think we're in the range of our guide, but obviously, we're at the low end of it. So I think it's hard to come off of a 4% on a 5-year guide and then get yourself back into 6% to 8%. So it's our belief that we continue to be at the low end of that guide.

But that's -- our job right now is to maximize new IOL launches to extend our equipment presence to get into higher-growth categories and try and find the ways that we can grow our business beyond the market growth that's obviously not where we would like it to be right now. So -- but that's partly why we're entering new categories, right? We got Valeda out there. We've got BRYTLY out there. ENCELTO, those are all new white space areas for us. And then you've got all the new IOLs coming, which I think help us I think you've got continued movement in equipment that drives this bit.

So take it in aggregate, we probably have 10, 12 new products all of which are adding some degree of growth, many of which are concentrating now on the fastest segments of what we're doing and importantly, getting into white space. So what we need to do is perform with those, execute well against those and try and grow our way regardless of what the markets do. That's really where we're focused. My sense is we can get into and stay in the range, but it will likely be the bottom of the range.

Operator: Our next question is from Steve Lichtman with William Blair.

Steven Lichtman: David, just going back on contact lenses on the price contribution, the 3% currently, you mentioned not sustainable. What level do you think is sustainable and should we be factoring in? And how does that differ U.S. versus what you're seeing OUS?

David Endicott: Yes. I mean the U.S. is more sustainable in price, internationally is less. And the fundamentals are pretty basic, right? I mean it's -- the online market is squeezing the chains. The chains are then resisting price and online has always resisted price. You're going to get a little bit there, but you're just not going to get what we used to get. In the U.S., it's still predominantly an independent OD market. So you can still pass on price. The customer pass -- our optometrist community passes that price along. And the chains are relatively receptive in the U.S. still because it's probably 60% independents and 40% chains and online. It's exactly the opposite internationally.

So I think what you should expect is that price is not as strong, but I think you'll get some. And again, I will have to see how the consumer fares over the next couple of months. We've already taken a price increase in this business. So we'll watch that for next year and see what happens.

Steven Lichtman: That's helpful. And then, Tim, on the efficiency programs, are the incremental savings you mentioned coming on the manufacturing side or OpEx? And how much of the now $130 million in savings are you going to be capturing in 2026?

Timothy Stonesifer: Yes. I would say that it's a combination of areas. It's -- we continue to drive productivity in our manufacturing operations and footprint to your point. I would say that's a good chunk of it. We've also made some structural changes in R&D due to the discontinuation of the PowerVision project that we talked about last quarter. And then just looking across the business, all the teams are identifying additional opportunities. So we feel very good about the program. And as we said when we first came out, we called about $100 million of run rate savings, and now we think it's going to be about $130 million of run rate savings.

As far as the additional $30 million and how much of that hits this year, I'd say a small piece will. I say, I would think a majority of that will hit next year.

Operator: Our next question is from Issie Kirby with Redburn.

Issie Kirby: I wanted to ask about the Neurotech acquisition and your commercial strategy here. Will you be leveraging your existing sales force? Any expansion needed? And then also when Aurion eventually comes to market, just thinking about what commercial investments you might need to make there? And then I have a follow-up.

David Endicott: Yes, Issie, on Neurotech, they're pretty well situated. They're a year into the launch, and we'll probably complement what they're doing with some more resource. But I think mostly what we're going to try and do is coordinate. And obviously, we have a fairly substantial retina sales force already that I think can help guide and introduce and coordinate with them to try and help relationships and some of the connections with the ASCs that they want to work with. But I think of that as just kind of free help, if you will, because it's not any incremental cost.

I do think we'll add a little bit of resource to their business overall just because it looks like a good opportunity for us. And then on the Aurion launch, I would say most of what we're going to do there commercially has not yet been developed. So we're still months away from an approval at least. And so I think if we're kind of in that back half of '28, I see that as an approval timing. I would think we'll need to be putting things together really next year, those will all be incremental costs.

But I would say they are planned in right now as we think about next year, and we'll guide on that as we get into the beginning of February.

Issie Kirby: Great. And then on AT-IOLs, is the way you're going to market or certainly marketing changing at all, given how much more competitive it is, particularly in the U.S. You mentioned you'll include sort of direct clinical comparisons with Vivity Pro. Just how are you thinking about your go-to-market with advanced firewalls in a more competitive space?

David Endicott: Yes, it's a really good question. There is -- yes, the short answer is yes, we're doing 2 or 3 things actually. One of the things we're doing is we are speeding up the -- you'll see that over the last 18 months, we've sped up the innovation pace. So we have -- we've got PanOptix Pro out. We got TruPlus out. We got Vivity Pro out all really within the last 24 months or so. We've got another 2 lenses behind that, that we will appropriately launch based on the timing that we see the market would be receptive.

I think in addition to that, I think what we've done is we've done some direct-to-patient work that's mostly online work, but I think it's a different go-to-market strategy than we've had in the past, which is to try and articulate to patients what the differences are in these lenses and where -- what their preferences might be and how those could be satisfied. And I think further to that point, we've also spent a good bit of time thinking about with new products, what are we comparing to, so that we have not just -- my lens is better than your lens, but good data that says here's the difference in near vision actually in a direct comparison.

Here's the difference in intermediate vision actually. And here's the difference, if there is one, and there isn't, in many cases, on distance and in contrast because we're quite concerned about the misinformation, I think, that's going on at least in some of the initial launches.

Operator: Our next question is from David Saxon with Needham & Company.

David Saxon: So first, maybe I'll do Tryptyr, and then I'll have a follow-up. So I think last quarter, Tryptyr was kind of in the high teens in dollar terms. So did that get into the 20s this quarter? And how are you feeling about driving volumes next year? And also, how should we think about kind of gross to net dynamics over the next, call it, 12 months?

David Endicott: Yes. Look, Tryptyr is going well. I mean we're -- our volumes are kind of on pace to what we'd hoped for. I think we saw something like 11,000 unique prescribers last month. We've got 2/3 of the commercial lives covered at this point. And our share, I think, we're -- we've gained just short, I think, of about 6% this month or last month. And so I feel like we're doing exactly what we need to do. We've got more work to do on reimbursement. We need to pick up another Medicare plan at least. And I do think there's still some commercial work we can do. But what we're most excited about is getting the DTC outgoing.

We needed to kind of get over a certain threshold with commercial to make that viable. We initiated that last month. And I think what you're seeing is a real positive response to the product itself from the -- from the physicians that are prescribing it. And that's been -- I think our most important idea has been, look, what are you seeing with the patients and they're seeing very quick response, which is what we had hoped for and a very kind of meaningful tolerance, which is really a big deal, too. Because I think patients will really want resolved kind of comfort.

And I think the data that we showed at the optometry and ophthalmology meetings on Tryptyr, I think, gives us real comfort that what we had hoped to see with Tryptyr is exactly what they're seeing. And we were hearing that from the docs, but it's really great to see it in both the docs feedback and then also the data that we've created.

David Saxon: Okay. Great. And then I wanted to follow up on just your comments around the next round of IOL launches. I mean you have PanOptix Pro and Vivity Pro out there, Vivity's coming out. But you just discontinued PowerVision last quarter. So how do we think about kind of that next leg of IOL launches as it relates to kind of what you have out there in the market or getting out and what's already out there from a competitive perspective? And then also, just kind of general level of confidence in the U.S. penetration, AT-IOL penetration getting into the 30%, 40% range that you've talked about historically?

David Endicott: Yes. Okay. So on the lenses themselves, look, I feel very confident that we probably have the world's most successful optical design engineers. And I do believe what you see in PanOptix and then PanOptix Pro and Vivity and Vivity Pro. And we have follow-ons for both of those products that advance those designs even further. So again, we're traveling towards lower optical disturbances with the trifocals and the detractive lenses. And then we're traveling closer and closer to better near, better intermediate with our -- with the EDOF lenses. And I think we are going to be in front of most people on this, and it's not that they won't catch up eventually.

But I think we are certainly going to lead the way as we go forward on those designs and those lenses. Now there's -- we obviously entered last quarter an agreement with the RxSight folks. We think they've got a great idea in adjustability. We've got some great ideas around what we could do to create presbyopic resolution. And together, I think we can come up with something that's really exciting. So that's our next kind of phase after that. And then we've got a lot of irons in the fire around the world on other kinds of designs and ideas. And I would just -- I'd be a little bit hesitant to kind of comment on those yet.

They're generally pretty early in their work, but we're excited about that stuff. On AT-IOL penetration, I do think that the confidence we have on the long term is built off of kind of an annual survey we do around what the consumer willingness to pay is. It generally is hovered kind of in the 35% to 40% of patients given the right information are willing to compensate for the AT-IOL, PC-IOL one in particular. What I think is important is that you do see these kind of run-ups when you see new products. So this most recent run-up, I would attribute largely to the amount of competitive promotion going on in the U.S.

But the international one, again, that's pretty steady right now. And I think you see kind of the steady march that has historically been kind of 50 basis points a year has accelerated most recently, closer to 100. I expect it will probably settle back at some point, but it's going to be a kind of steady march towards, I think, kind of low 30s, ultimately peaking somewhere in the mid-30s.

Operator: Our next question is from Tom Stephan with Stifel.

Thomas Stephan: First one on 2027, I guess the way I'm kind of reading it, you sound pretty confident in maybe 4% to 5% organic growth next year on revs. But this year is tracking, maybe only a bit above that on the guide organically. Next year, you lap UNITY, so that will be a pretty meaningful headwind. So I guess my question is, what gets you next year to maybe 4% to 5%? As we think about other segments in the biz outside of equipment that would need to accelerate from '26 to '27, I think you called out Implantables, but what else accelerated organically from a growth rate standpoint next year versus this year? And then I have a follow-up.

David Endicott: Well, let me start by saying, look, our -- during this stretch where the market growth is more modest, our desire right now is to focus on executing more effectively in things like the IOL launches. So if you -- if you think about what we're trying to do, we're trying to maximize our IOL launches, particularly Vivity Pro, TruPlus and then also PanOptix Pro around the world and get into this high premiumization idea where the segment of the market we're participating in is growing considerably faster than the average total market aggregated. That's what we're doing with that. That's what we're doing with daily disposables. That's why we're concentrating on artificial tiers and OTC.

That's why we're concentrating on dry eye and Rx. Those are categories that are all growing faster by a lot than the market. So if we rotate our promotion in that direction and we enter new categories like Valeda with dry AMD, like Voyager with glaucoma, like BRYTLY with a whitener, like an ENCELTO. Those are all new white spaces for us.

So I'm just -- what I'm trying to direct you towards is that if we shift our mix towards the faster part of the market that's growing the fastest, we avail ourselves of faster-growing TAM than when we aggregate ourselves into some of the slower-growing markets, which, again, look like monofocal cataract some of the other kinds of businesses that we're in, reusable lenses et cetera. So that's the principal way in which we're going to get there. But I will also just point to BRYTLY is a new product, UNITY M, UNITY DX, ENCELTO. We've got a couple of other contact lenses.

We've got a new contact lens coming -- and we've got UNITY -- sorry, Vivity Pro, all coming -- those are all new products for us next year that add to year one revenue.

Thomas Stephan: Got it. That's great. And then quickly on my follow-up, just for equipment. Nice to see, again, strong year-over-year growth. But a little surprising, seeing res down sequentially in the third quarter. I know there's seasonality, but the UNITY launch is still early days, especially CS, not really getting going until the second quarter, and it sounds like Valeda is continuing to ramp. So David, kind of talk about what happened in the quarter with equipment what you saw from kind of an end market standpoint as it relates to possibly higher interest rates? And what does that kind of pretend for 4Q and sort of the near term?

David Endicott: Yes. Well, first thing is just remember, the comp last year was 27% growth or something like that. I might have that partially correct, but it's in the high 20s. And I think what you're really seeing right now is more of a steady -- we're moving into a steady state of reasonable growth. It's going to be somewhere in the high single digits to the low double digits as we kind of move forward, depending on what we're launching when. So I think the exciting part of where we are with CS and VCS is we are kind of working our way through a backlog of really kind of older equipment that needs to be replaced.

Now the replacement cycle, people -- some markets, let's read Japan, in particular, has been a little slower than we had hoped for. But other markets like the U.S. have been particularly good. So I think we've seen kind of on balance what we would have expected, given all of the equipment that we're launching. And again, I feel pretty good about the leads we've got, the visibility to our funnel is solid. We're looking at the fourth quarter, and I think we feel pretty good about that. So again, I see next year as principally a continuation of what we had always said, which is first year will be very strong.

Second year would be a little -- will be similarly strong, and then it will settle into a cadence that is year-on-year, roughly representing the amount of equipment that retires which, again, would be about 10% to 12% of the total installed base. So that's kind of the way we see it.

Operator: We have reached the end of the question-and-answer session. I would like to turn the floor back over to Dan Cravens for closing comments.

Daniel Cravens: Thanks, Max, and thanks again for joining us today. If anybody has any follow-up questions, certainly reach out to the IR team for investors or our core comp team for media. I know there are a couple of analysts that didn't get questions in, but we'll be sure to address those in the follow-up calls. Again, thanks again for your time, and look forward to connecting with you.

Operator: This concludes today's teleconference. You may disconnect your lines at this time. Thank you for your participation.

#3171. Apple reportedly met with Thai officials over spyware alerts sent to politicians

Bloomberg reports that Apple has met with Thai government officials in the wake of its recent wave of iPhone alerts about mercenary spyware attacks. Here are the details.

Last week, The Financial Times and TechCrunch reported that Apple had sent a fresh wave of threat notifications to potential spyware targets in 99 countries, warning them that they may have been targeted by mercenary spyware attacks.

At the time, the FT focused on German lawmakers who had received the warnings, while TechCrunch highlighted recipients in other countries, including Beirut-based filmmaker Radwan Mortada.

Today, Bloomberg reported that “Thailand held meetings with Apple Inc. officials” over the notifications, adding that the warnings raised questions about “who may have targeted [Thai politicians] and why.”

Receiving an alert doesn’t necessarily mean a device was successfully compromised, Digital Economy and Society Minister Chaichanok Chidchob said after meeting Apple representatives Wednesday, Krungthep Turakij and other media reported. Thai authorities also have no evidence so far that the latest attempted attacks involved Pegasus, the spyware developed by Israel’s NSO Group, he said.

As Bloomberg explains, Pegasus was “allegedly used against pro-democracy campaigners in 2022.”

The recent wave of alerts, which were sent out on October 29, followed another round in August, when Apple notified potential targets in 110 countries. As always, Apple declined to disclose what triggers these notifications to prevent attackers from evading detection in the future, but recommended that recipients enable Lockdown Mode and seek expert security assistance.

Bloomberg added that Thai authorities are expected to meet with other technology companies on Thursday to discuss potential countermeasures, including risks to Android devices.

To read Bloomberg’s full report, follow this link.

#3169. Centrus' Backlog Hit $5.4 Billion. Its Quarterly Revenue Was $55 Million. Here's How Those Numbers Fit Together.

Investors shouldn't conflate its backlog with its actual revenue.

Centrus Energy (LEU +2.09%) is a linchpin of the nuclear energy market. It's one of the few U.S. companies licensed to sell low-enriched uranium (LEU), the most common fuel for conventional nuclear reactors. It's also the only publicly traded U.S. producer of high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) for next-gen nuclear reactors.

Centrus' contingent LEU and HALEU backlog swelled to $5.4 billion at the end of the third quarter of 2026, up from $3.0 billion in the second quarter. However, it only generated $55.5 million in revenue in the third quarter. In the first nine months of 2026, it generated $308.3 million in revenue, and it expects that figure to reach $450-$500 million for the full year. Let's see why there's such a huge gap between its backlog and reported revenue.

Centrus' growing backlog looks impressive, but those commitments extend through 2040. Meanwhile, its quarterly and annual revenues include only the orders it delivers, bills, and recognizes under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) within that period.

Nuclear power utilities also typically secure their supply chains years in advance through long-term contracts. So while Centrus is locking in more contracts, they won't necessarily boost its near-term revenue. Instead, analysts expect Centrus' annual revenue to grow at only a 3-year CAGR of 2.6%, from $448.7 million in 2025 to $484.5 million in 2028. They expect its net income to decline from $77.8 million in 2025 to $66.9 million in 2028.

Some major changes will also throttle Centrus' near-term growth. About 13 years ago, Centrus stopped enriching its own LEU in the U.S. after it became cheaper to import LEU from overseas and resell it to U.S. utilities. But in recent years, the sanctions against Russia and the U.S. push toward energy independence drove Centrus to restart its domestic LEU plants.

The U.S. plans to ban all Russian uranium imports by 2028, before Centrus can fully restart its domestic LEU operations or ramp up HALEU production. That's why its growth will remain sluggish over the next few years, even as the nuclear energy market expands.

With an enterprise value of $3.4 billion, Centrus might seem reasonably valued at seven times this year's sales. However, it faces more near-term challenges than many other nuclear companies that aren't undergoing massive, capital-intensive transformations. I'd keep an eye on this stock, but I wouldn't buy it before other more promising nuclear power stocks.

#3168. Binance warns iPhone crypto holders of security flaw researchers say remains unpatched

Crypto exchange Binance has warned iPhone users about an iOS vulnerability that could allow malicious apps to access sensitive data stored by other apps. Here are the details.

In a post published on X (via AppleInsider), Binance says that a vulnerability called worse_query could allow “malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem.”

Binance says the flaw affects iOS 26.7.1, iOS 27.0.1, and iOS 27.2. However, a Community Note points out that researchers describe the vulnerability as an unpatched zero-day and that Apple’s latest security updates, including iOS 27.2.1 (the current version at the time of writing), do not mention a fix.

A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.…

That said, in addition to updating their devices, Binance recommends that iPhone crypto holders take the following immediate actions:

The vulnerability was disclosed by security researchers @0xjohnny and @forcequitOS, who published a proof of concept on GitHub demonstrating how it can be used to bypass iOS sandbox protections, which normally prevent apps from accessing each other’s files.

Researcher @forcequitOS also noted that neither iOS 27.2.1 nor iOS 27.3 beta 1 patches the vulnerability.

Just as a general statement so there isn’t any confusion about it, worse_query is *not* patched in iOS 27.2.1 and 27.3 beta 1. I’ll update version support on the readme when it’s patched.

Although the researcher describes the code as intended for developers and not useful on its own, other developers have already built apps using it, including a file manager that can access, modify, and delete data belonging to other apps without requiring a jailbreak.

According to The Hacker News, neither Binance nor the researchers have reported any attacks or cryptocurrency thefts involving the vulnerability so far.

Google has spent the past year making Gemini smarter, more capable and better connected to the apps and services people use every day. But one of its most useful features might also be one of its most personal: memory.

As Gemini has evolved, it's gotten better at remembering details from previous conversations, picking up where you left off and helping with ongoing projects. That's convenient, especially if you use the chatbot regularly, but it also raises an important question: How much does Gemini actually remember about you?

Until now, managing Gemini's memory hasn't always been straightforward. Google has offered controls for reviewing and deleting chat activity, but understanding what the chatbot has learned about you is another matter.

That's where Gemini's new Memory summary comes in. The feature gives users a clearer look at the information Gemini remembers about them, along with the ability to make changes.

Here's how to find your Memory summary, see what Gemini remembers and take control of the information it uses to personalize your conversations.

Google has begun rolling out its new “Memory summary” feature in Gemini for users who work with the chatbot through its desktop and mobile browser versions (it doesn’t seem to be working with the mobile Gemini app at the moment, however). And with this update comes the ability for users to take a look at what Gemini remembers about them and edit it to add more details about themselves or delete it as a whole.

The Memory summary doesn’t just feature a massive info dump that’s all about you—it actually summarizes everything it remembers about you via bullet points that detail your background, relationships, work, interests and preferences. After observing everything Gemini has learned about you and retained as the data it has gained from your previous conversations.
